title: Smithsonian's Lonnie Bunch to Step Down After White House Clash Over History
summary:
Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution's leader since 2019, announced Tuesday he will step down at the end of the year, capping a turbulent period in which the White House sought to reshape how American history is presented in the nation's museums.

Bunch's departure comes two months after a White House report branded the leadership of the Smithsonian—especially at the National Museum of American History—as "radical activists" who cannot be trusted. The report argued that the museum's portrayal of history wasn't "inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic." Anthea M. Hartig, the museum's first female director, faced growing scrutiny from President Trump and Republicans over the summer.

Unlike other cultural institutions, such as the Kennedy Center where Trump became chairman through a supportive board, the Smithsonian operates independently of the executive branch. Museum directors report to Bunch, who answers to a Board of Regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, and bipartisan lawmakers. Roberts, the Smithsonian's chancellor, praised Bunch for pursuing "excellence in the telling of our nation's story."

Bunch said he leaves with "very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude." The White House did not immediately comment.

This clash highlights a broader debate: Who gets to decide how history is told? Museums are often battlegrounds for cultural and political values. Bunch, a historian who previously founded the National Museum of African American History and Culture, has been a prominent figure in making museums more inclusive. His departure signals that the Trump administration may install leadership more aligned with its vision.

For kids like you, this matters because the stories you hear in museums shape how you understand your country. Whether it's tales of presidents or pioneers, the way they're told can change. As Bunch leaves, the question remains: What story will the Smithsonian tell next?
why_it_matters: Museums are among the most trusted places where the public learns history, so whoever leads them decides which stories are presented as truly American. A political shift in museum leadership could change what future generations learn about slavery, presidents, protest, and national identity.

background_read: The Smithsonian Institution, created by Congress, is a national museum and research network that relies on public as well as private support.

Lonnie Bunch, the first African American to lead the Smithsonian, was also the founding director of its National Museum of African American History and Culture, a museum devoted to Black history and culture.

The National Museum of American History, directed by Anthea M. Hartig, holds many of the country’s best-known artifacts and often sits at the center of arguments over how the nation tells its own story.

Part of the Smithsonian’s design is to sit outside direct White House control: its leader reports to a Board of Regents that includes the vice president, the chief justice, and lawmakers from both parties.

Presidents and politicians have still pressured it throughout its history, because whatever is displayed in a national museum sends a message about which people, events, and ideas are treated as important.

perspectives.description: They want federally supported museums to emphasize pride, unity, and what they see as an inspiring national story. In their view, leaders like Bunch have allowed activism to crowd out that mission.

They worry that Bunch’s departure will pressure museums to soften difficult history about racism, injustice, and inequality. They argue that honest storytelling is patriotic and that the White House should not control curators.

The Smithsonian was designed to have some independence from the president, so changing its direction takes time and involves boards, budgets, and political pressure. Bunch’s resignation is important, but it is not the same as a direct takeover.

The next Smithsonian secretary will test whether a federally funded institution can resist political pressure. How the board handles that choice will shape whether future museum exhibits reflect one political vision or a broader range of American experiences.
